summary: A humorous April 1st memo that proposes requirements for an imaginary Omniscience Protocol, to support legislative efforts to interfere with allegedly illegal activity online. It is a satire of such proposals, not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st memo satirizes proposals for monitoring users' computers. It describes an imaginary protocol with requirements that are deliberately impossible.

questions: what are the omniscience protocol requirements
subtitle: An April 1st satire listing impossible requirements for an Omniscience Protocol.

tldr.problem: This April 1st satire imagines enforcement systems needing to distinguish illegal activity from innocent behavior and determine a user's intent.
tldr.mechanism: It lists requirements for a client installed on users' computers that answers queries from enforcement servers.
tldr.outcome: The requirements include contradictory and implausible demands; this is a joke, not a real protocol design.

today: RFC 3751 is an Informational April 1st satire about the imagined Omniscience Protocol. It is not a real protocol specification.

sections.title: The Omniscience Protocol Premise
sections.content:
The memo refers to public discussion of ways to interfere with allegedly illegal online activity. It argues that enforcement would need to distinguish wrongdoers from innocent users and determine intent.

It then proposes requirements for an imaginary Omniscience Protocol (OP). The document is satire, not a technical specification for a real service.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC imagines a system that could know what a computer user intended. The impossible premise is used to make fun of surveillance proposals.

sections.title: Clients and Enforcement Servers
sections.content:
The imagined design uses a client on the user's computer and servers run by law or copyright enforcement organizations. Clients register with servers for their jurisdiction when the computer starts, and servers send queries on their chosen schedule.

The memo says future versions might use peer-to-peer operation. It presents this as a possibility in its fictional design.
sections.plainLanguage: In the imagined setup, a computer client reports to enforcement servers. The servers send questions to the client.

sections.title: Operational and Functional Requirements
sections.content:
Operational requirements include installing clients over users' objections, hiding them from users and virus detectors, communicating through firewalls and NATs or while disconnected, and resisting spoofing.

Functional requirements demand that the client determine intent, distinguish legal copies from illegal ones even if modified, identify who placed files on a device, protect unrelated private information, and apply the laws of the device's location. The RFC's security section concludes with “Good luck.”
sections.plainLanguage: The wish list asks for software that is invisible, cannot be fooled, knows intent, and never invades unrelated privacy. The closing “Good luck” signals the satire.
